identity.title: Focal neurologic deficit (limb weakness, aphasia, Horner) accompanying chest/back pain

technique.how: In any patient with acute chest, back or abdominal pain, screen for a focal deficit: speech, facial symmetry, limb strength and drift in all four limbs, sensation, and pupils/ptosis (Horner). Note paraplegia (spinal artery), hemiparesis/aphasia (carotid), and limb ischaemia. Compare with pulse and BP in both arms.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to cooperate; otherwise use observed asymmetry.

interpretation.positive_finding: A focal neurological deficit in a patient with acute chest/back pain raises the probability of aortic dissection (pooled LR+ 4.4, specificity 95%); stroke-like presentation with pain should prompt aortic imaging before thrombolysis.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of a deficit does little to exclude dissection: only about 17% of confirmed dissections have focal deficits.
interpretation.pitfalls: Deficits may be transient or fluctuate and be attributed to primary stroke; pain may be absent in dissection presenting as stroke. Syncope with deficit can be misread as seizure.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: treat as dissection until imaged (CT angiography), avoid anticoagulation/thrombolysis; negative: does not lower dissection probability meaningfully.

estimates.population: Adults with suspected acute aortic dissection in 9 studies (n=2400); prevalence across studies 21.9%-76.1% (mean 39.1%)
estimates.reference_standard: Confirmed dissection by imaging/surgery/autopsy as defined in included studies (not detailed in abstract)
estimates.quote: neurologic deficit (n = 3, specificity = 95%, positive likelihood ratio [LR+] = 4.4, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.3-5.7, I2 = 0%)

estimates.target_condition: Acute thoracic aortic dissection (finding: focal neurological deficit) - pooled sensitivity from case series
estimates.population: Consecutive patients with confirmed thoracic aortic dissection (21 studies, >=18 patients each)
estimates.reference_standard: Confirmed thoracic aortic dissection (imaging, surgery or autopsy)
estimates.quote: 31% have pulse deficits or blood pressure differentials, and 17% have focal neurological deficits

sources.citation: Ohle R, Kareemi HK, Wells G, Perry JJ. Clinical Examination for Acute Aortic Dissection: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2018;25(4):397-412.
Klompas M. Does this patient have an acute thoracic aortic dissection? JAMA. 2002;287(17):2262-2272.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of a deficit to lower suspicion; do not delay aortic imaging in a stroke-like presentation with chest/back pain.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Neurologic deficit with chest pain, pulse deficit, or hypotension is a time-critical emergency: immediate CT angiography and surgical/vascular consultation.

extraction_notes: Neither full text is open access (JAMA, Acad Emerg Med); locations are 'Abstract, Results'. Ohle reports specificity 95% and LR+ 4.4 (3.3-5.7) but no sensitivity or LR- for neurologic deficit, and sensitivity must not be derived from an LR -> partially_quantified. Klompas reports LR+ for neurological deficits as a between-study range 6.6-33.0 (Abstract) - not entered as a point value; only the pooled sensitivity 17% is entered (case-series design, so prevalence null). Ohle prevalence 'ranged from 21.9% to 76.1% (mean +/- SD = 39.1% +/- 17.1%)' (Abstract) is a mean across studies, not a cohort prevalence, so left null. PubMed lists Ohle as 2019; print issue is Acad Emerg Med 2018;25(4).
